passage: From the window of my flat I can see the nursery school's courtyard, and every morning I watch Aadhya, five, walk in and go straight to the bench where Ira waits. Aadhya sits so close their sleeves touch, and swings her legs in time with Ira's. Today, though, after a quarrel over the red bucket, Aadhya sat at the far end of the bench, looking at the sand. By lunch she had shuffled back next to Ira. I can't say what they said to each other.

qa.q: Where does Aadhya go every morning?
qa.a: She goes straight to the bench where Ira waits.

qa.q: What might Aadhya's choice of seats say about how she felt today?
qa.a: Sitting at the far end after the quarrel suggests she was upset with Ira, and shuffling back by lunch suggests the quarrel had eased. Kids also move seats for fun, so it's only a guess.

qa.q: What could an adult watching do if a child keeps sitting apart from a friend?
qa.a: They can watch the pattern over several days before deciding anything, and stay ready to help if the child seems upset.

qa.q: How might Ira feel when Aadhya sits at the far end?
qa.a: Ira may feel unsure or a little hurt, and glad when Aadhya returns to sit close again.

grounding: Sitting close shows liking and comfort, while shifting away can show a quarrel, seen by an observer who can only guess.

passage:
Day one: at the Bristol nursery, Jyoti, five, walked into the reading corner and sat down right next to Rehana. Their knees touched as they looked at the same book.
Day three: Jyoti chose the beanbag across the room and pulled out a puzzle. Rehana didn't say anything but went to the shelf by herself.
Day five: after a shared snack, Jyoti dragged her cushion beside Rehana again and whispered, "Can I see your page?" Rehana shifted over to make space.

qa.q: What did Jyoti do on day five to sit next to Rehana?
qa.a: She dragged her cushion beside Rehana.

qa.q: What might Jyoti's move to the beanbag on day three suggest, and what does the pattern of days add?
qa.a: The move might mean a quarrel or a wish to be apart, but she chose the puzzle, so it might just have been for fun. Coming back to sit close on day five suggests she still likes Rehana.

qa.q: What could the teacher do if a child keeps changing seats?
qa.a: The teacher can watch the pattern over several days, and check in gently if a child seems left out or upset.

qa.q: How might Rehana feel when Jyoti sits beside her again?
qa.a: She may feel pleased and reassured, since she moved over to make space.

grounding: Choosing a seat beside a friend shows liking and comfort, and patterns across days matter more than one moment.

passage: Rain meant lunch in the cramped hall, benches jammed together. For weeks Pema had squeezed in beside Dawa every single day. This was the third day she had sat at the far end instead, eating alone, her back half-turned. Vaibhav Sir noticed the pattern, not just the moment. He sat down near her with his tiffin. “You and Dawa usually sit together.” Pema poked her rice. “She broke my blue crayon and didn't say sorry.” Sir nodded. “Shall we talk to her after lunch?”

qa.q: How many days had Pema sat at the far end?
qa.a: This was the third day.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling as she sat at the far end with her back half-turned?
qa.a: She was hurt and cross with Dawa about the broken crayon and the missing sorry, and was keeping her distance.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Vaibhav Sir to notice the pattern rather than one lunch?
qa.a: Children change seats for fun, so one day means little, but three days away from her usual friend showed something was wrong.

qa.q: How might Dawa see Pema sitting far away?
qa.a: Dawa might feel confused or left out, perhaps not realising the crayon mattered so much.

grounding: A teacher notices a pattern of a child shifting away from her usual friend and finds a quarrel behind it.

passage: Every morning in the city nursery, Gautam sat next to Nikhil. On Monday he sat by the window instead. Rukmini Ma'am felt a flicker of worry and watched. On Tuesday he sat by the door; on Wednesday, under the fan. Each time he grinned at Nikhil across the room, and Nikhil grinned back. At playtime they were inseparable. On Thursday Gautam announced, “Today I'm sitting on the moon seat!” and plopped down right next to Nikhil again. Rukmini laughed. It was just a game.

qa.q: Where did Gautam sit on Wednesday?
qa.a: Under the fan.

qa.q: What did Gautam's grin across the room suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggested he felt happy, playful and still friendly with Nikhil; moving seats was a game, not a quarrel.

qa.q: What would you advise a teacher who sees a child suddenly change seats?
qa.a: Watch for a few days and look at other signs, like grins and playtime, before deciding there is a problem.

qa.q: How might Rukmini Ma'am have felt on Monday?
qa.a: She felt a small worry that the friends had fallen out, until the pattern showed otherwise.

grounding: A preschooler changes seats for fun, and the teacher watches the pattern rather than one moment.

passage:
“Uday! Sit next to me!” Divyansh patted the chair at the birthday table.
Uday hesitated, then sat. “Okay.”
“We're best friends, so we sit together.”
They shared crisps. Then Divyansh grabbed the last one.
“Hey! That was mine!”
“No, mine!”
Uday picked up his plate and moved two chairs away.
Divyansh looked at the empty chair. After a minute he held out half a crisp. “Sorry. Come back?”
Uday looked at the crisp, then at him, and scooted back. “Only if we share the cake.”

qa.q: What did Divyansh hold out after Uday moved?
qa.a: Half a crisp.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling when he looked at the empty chair?
qa.a: He probably felt sorry and lonely without Uday beside him, and wanted to make up.

qa.q: What small step fixed the quarrel?
qa.a: Divyansh said sorry and offered half a crisp, which invited Uday back.

qa.q: How did Uday show his feelings by where he sat?
qa.a: He moved two chairs away when he was annoyed about the crisp and scooted back when he felt friendly again.

grounding: Two preschoolers sit together to show liking and one shifts away during a quarrel, then returns after an apology.

passage:
Classroom note from Swati, end of the week

Bhavna sat next to her friend at the blue table every morning this week, knees touching, sharing crayons. On Tuesday she took a seat at the far end and kept her back turned. I asked quietly; they had argued over a glitter pen. By lunch they were side by side again.

On Thursday she swapped to the window seat, giggling, and her friend followed. That was just a game.

So one move doesn't worry me. The pattern tells me they are close. 🙂

qa.q: What did Bhavna and her friend argue over?
qa.a: A glitter pen.

qa.q: What was Bhavna probably feeling when she sat at the far end with her back turned on Tuesday?
qa.a: She was most likely upset and cross with her friend after their argument. By Thursday, swapping seats with giggles showed she felt playful, not upset.

qa.q: How did Swati make sense of Bhavna's seat changes?
qa.a: Swati asked quietly on Tuesday instead of guessing, and looked at the whole week's pattern rather than one moment.

qa.q: How does Bhavna's friend show they feel close to Bhavna?
qa.a: The friend shares crayons at the blue table and follows Bhavna to the window seat on Thursday.

grounding: It shows a preschooler sitting close to a favourite playmate, shifting away after a quarrel and swapping seats for fun, with the pattern mattering most.
